title: The Helpful Reply
intro: You complained online about a late order from Meridu Store. Now someone has replied.
This time you can talk back. Pick your replies and sniff each message as it arrives.
Every chat ends with your choice. Choose wisely.

notify.text: Sorry about your order! We can refund you here in DMs…

banner: Message request · you do not follow this account

msg.text: Hi! So sorry about your late order 😔

msg: . We can refund you right here in DMs.

replies.text: How do I get the refund?
Are you really Meridu? How can I check?

msg: Easy! Enter your card number on the page, then

msg.text: tell me the 6-digit code we text you

replies.text: Why would a refund need my card number and a code?

sys.text: The account changed its name to "Meridu Help (official)"

msg.text: Your refund expires in 10 minutes, so please hurry

replies.text: OK, I do not want to lose the refund
I will ask on Meridu's own website instead

msg: Totally safe, it is how all refunds work.

msg.text: Hundreds of customers did it today.

replies.text: I will contact Meridu through its own website first
No real refund needs my code. Block and report.

dmfirst.label: They messaged first
dmfirst.lens: You never contacted this account. It found your public complaint and messaged you.
dmfirst.why: Real companies answer in the open or through their own support page. Scammers watch public complaints.

link.label: Look-alike link
link.lens: This goes to meridu-refunds.help, not to Meridu's real site.
link.why: Never give card details on a page you reached through a message. Check where the link really goes.

code.label: Asks for your code
code.lens: It wants the code your bank texts you.
code.why: That code lets someone log in or pay as you. Anyone who asks for it is a scammer.

rename.label: It renamed itself
rename.lens: The account changed its name when you doubted it.
rename.why: Real companies do not change names to win your trust.

rush.label: Countdown pressure
rush.why: Rushing you is a pressure trick. Real refunds do not vanish in minutes.

everyone.label: "Everyone did it"
everyone.lens: It says hundreds of customers already did it.
everyone.why: A crowd you cannot see proves nothing.

logo.label: Shop logo
logo.why: Logos are easy to copy, so they prove nothing on their own.

hello.label: Friendly and sorry
hello.why: Being friendly is not suspicious by itself.

actions.label: Enter my card details and the code
Contact Meridu through its own website

block_report.line: Blocked and reported. The platform removed the fake account before it reached anyone else.

verify.line: Meridu's real website said: "We never ask for card details or codes in messages." Case cracked.

go_ahead.line: The code let Mirage pay from your account. The "refund" never came, and money left instead.

what_if.go_ahead: Asking "why does a refund need my code?" was the way out. The answer is: it never does.
what_if.verify: Checking was smart. Reporting the account as well gets it removed faster.

golden_rule: A refund never needs your card code. Contact the shop through its own website, not through a message.

quick_check.q: Someone replies to your public complaint and asks for your card number and a code texted to you. What is true?

options.text: Real shops do this to speed up refunds
It is fine if the account has a ✔ in its name
A refund never needs your codes, so it is a trap
Give the code but change your password later

quick_check.explain: Codes and card numbers are for paying, not for receiving money. That request alone tells you it is a trap.

hints.nudge: Why would a refund need a code from you?

rows.v: Card number and the code your bank texts
Through its own website or the contact details on your receipt

rows.v: Anyone who asks for it is a scammer
